name: VLANs
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Create VLANs, assign data and voice access ports, verify VLANs across switches and explain why VLANs need routing.

lesson.intro: A VLAN turns one physical switch into several separate LANs. It is one of the most tested ideas on the CCNA because almost everything else in Domain 2 (trunks, spanning tree, inter-VLAN routing) builds on it. In this lesson you will create VLANs, put PCs and IP phones into them, prove a VLAN really spans several switches, see how traffic gets between VLANs, and fix the classic 'wrong VLAN' fault.
objectives: Explain why a VLAN is a separate broadcast domain and a separate IP subnet
Create and name normal-range VLANs and assign access ports, including a data and voice VLAN on a phone port
Distinguish the default, data, voice, native, management and parking VLAN roles
Verify a VLAN across switches with show vlan, show interfaces status and the MAC address table
Explain the three ways hosts in different VLANs reach each other and troubleshoot a port in the wrong VLAN

sections.title: One switch, many LANs
sections.body:
Picture a 48-port switch on the second floor. Sales laptops, Engineering build servers and a guest printer are all plugged into it. With factory settings every port is in the same group, so when a Sales laptop sends a broadcast (an ARP request, a DHCP Discover), every device on the floor receives it, including the printer and the build servers. That whole group is one **broadcast domain**.

A **VLAN** (virtual LAN) splits that one switch into several logical switches. Ports you put in VLAN 10 exchange frames only with other VLAN 10 ports; ports in VLAN 20 live in their own world. A broadcast sent in VLAN 10 is flooded only out VLAN 10 ports (and trunks that carry VLAN 10), and the switch never forwards a frame from one VLAN into another. The MAC address table is kept per VLAN too, so the same switch can learn and forward for each VLAN independently.

Why bother? The official cert guide lists reasons worth knowing for the exam:

- Smaller broadcast domains mean less wasted bandwidth and CPU on every host.
- Security: sensitive hosts sit in their own VLAN, away from guests, and traffic between VLANs must pass a router where it can be filtered.
- Flexibility: group users by job, not by which closet their desk is wired to.
- Smaller failure domains: a broadcast storm or a misbehaving host stays inside one VLAN.
- Voice traffic can be kept apart from data so it can be prioritized.

The rule to carry into every later topic: **one VLAN = one broadcast domain = one IP subnet**. If a design has three VLANs, it has three subnets, and traffic between them must be routed.
sections.code:
SW1 (one physical switch)
   +-----------------------------------------+
   |  VLAN 10 (Sales)       VLAN 20 (Eng)    |
   |  Gi0/1   Gi0/2         Gi0/3   Gi0/4    |
   +----|-------|-------------|-------|------+
       PC1     PC2           PC3     PC4
     10.1.10.0/24          10.1.20.0/24

PC1 broadcast -> flooded to PC2 only (same VLAN)
PC1 -> PC3    -> needs a router (different subnet)
sections.tip: When an exam question lists VLANs, mentally write a subnet next to each one. Routing and DHCP questions get much easier.
sections.pitfall: Giving hosts in two different VLANs addresses from the same subnet. The hosts think they are local to each other and ARP directly, but the switch keeps the VLANs apart, so the ARP never arrives. Keep one subnet per VLAN.

check.question: A switch has ports in VLAN 10 and VLAN 20. PC1 in VLAN 10 sends an ARP broadcast. Which devices receive it?
choices: Every device on the switch, because ARP is a broadcast
Only devices on VLAN 10 ports (and trunks carrying VLAN 10)
Only the default gateway
Devices in VLAN 10 and VLAN 1, since VLAN 1 is the default
check.explanation: A VLAN is its own broadcast domain, so the switch floods the broadcast only out ports in VLAN 10, including trunks that carry VLAN 10. VLAN 20 ports never see it, and VLAN 1 is just another VLAN with no special view of other VLANs' traffic.

sections.title: VLAN numbers and the default VLAN
sections.body:
Every VLAN has a number, the VLAN ID. The 802.1Q tag that carries the ID between switches has a 12-bit field, so the usable range is 1 to 4094 (0 and 4095 are reserved). Cisco splits that range in two:

- **Normal range: 1 to 1005.** Every Catalyst switch supports these, and they are the VLANs the CCNA blueprint asks you to configure.
- **Extended range: 1006 to 4094.** Supported on most current switches, with some VTP restrictions.

A brand-new switch already has five VLANs. **VLAN 1** is the **default VLAN**: every port starts in it, which is why a switch works out of the box. VLAN 1 can be used, but it cannot be deleted or renamed. VLANs 1002 to 1005 are leftovers for FDDI and Token Ring; they cannot be deleted or used for ports, and show vlan brief marks them act/unsup (active, unsupported).

VLAN 1 also carries control traffic by default (protocols such as CDP, VTP, DTP and PAgP), and it is the default native VLAN on trunks and the default management VLAN (interface vlan 1). Because every switch everywhere uses it, best practice is to move user ports out of VLAN 1 and keep the native and management VLANs on other numbers too. Anyone who plugs into an unconfigured port lands in VLAN 1, so leaving users there makes an intruder's job easy.

The example shows a factory-default 2960 with 24 FastEthernet and 2 Gigabit ports, all in VLAN 1. show vlan (without brief) prints the same list plus a second table of VLAN types and MTUs, which you can usually ignore.
sections.code:
SW1# show vlan brief

VLAN Name                             Status    Ports
---- -------------------------------- --------- -------------------------------
1    default                          active    Fa0/1, Fa0/2, Fa0/3, Fa0/4
                                                Fa0/5, Fa0/6, Fa0/7, Fa0/8
                                                Fa0/9, Fa0/10, Fa0/11, Fa0/12
                                                Fa0/13, Fa0/14, Fa0/15, Fa0/16
                                                Fa0/17, Fa0/18, Fa0/19, Fa0/20
                                                Fa0/21, Fa0/22, Fa0/23, Fa0/24
                                                Gi0/1, Gi0/2
1002 fddi-default                     act/unsup
1003 token-ring-default               act/unsup
1004 fddinet-default                  act/unsup
1005 trnet-default                    act/unsup
sections.tip: Normal-range VLANs are stored in flash:vlan.dat. With the default VTP mode they do not even appear in the running config, so erase startup-config alone does not remove them; on a lab switch you also delete vlan.dat and reload.
sections.pitfall: Thinking VLAN 1 is protected because it is the default. It is the opposite: every unconfigured port joins it, so user and management traffic in VLAN 1 is the easiest to reach.

check.question: Which statement about VLAN 1 on a Cisco switch is true?
choices: It can be deleted once all ports are moved out of it
It is an extended-range VLAN
It can be used for ports but cannot be deleted
It cannot be assigned to access ports
check.explanation: VLAN 1 is the default VLAN: every port starts in it, it can carry traffic, and it cannot be deleted or renamed. It is in the normal range (1 to 1005), not the extended range.

sections.title: Creating VLANs and access ports
sections.body:
An **access port** belongs to exactly one data VLAN and connects to an end device: a PC, printer, server or AP. The device sends ordinary untagged Ethernet frames and has no idea VLANs exist; the switch simply treats everything arriving on that port as part of the port's access VLAN.

The configuration is three ideas:

- `vlan 10` in global configuration mode creates the VLAN and enters VLAN configuration mode, where `name SALES` labels it. Names are optional; the default name is VLAN0010.
- `switchport mode access` makes the port always an access port. It also turns off DTP, so the port can never negotiate itself into a trunk.
- `switchport access vlan 10` assigns the port to VLAN 10.

Use `interface range` to configure many ports at once. If you assign a port to a VLAN that does not exist yet, IOS creates the VLAN for you and says so: `% Access VLAN does not exist. Creating vlan 30`. Then verify with show vlan brief, which lists every VLAN and its access ports. Trunk ports are not listed there, because they belong to many VLANs at once.

Two related commands round this out. `no vlan 30` deletes a VLAN (its ports are not moved anywhere; see the pitfall). `shutdown vlan 30` (or `shutdown` inside VLAN configuration mode) keeps the VLAN but stops the switch forwarding in it locally, shown as act/lshut.

Where does the configuration live? The interface commands appear in the running config under each interface as usual. The VLANs themselves are stored in the VLAN database, flash:vlan.dat. With VTP in its default server mode, the vlan 10 and name lines do not even show up in show running-config; in VTP transparent or off mode they do. Either way, show vlan brief is the source of truth for which VLANs exist.
sections.code:
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name SALES
SW1(config-vlan)# vlan 20
SW1(config-vlan)# name ENG
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range gigabitethernet0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# interface gigabitethernet0/3
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show vlan brief

VLAN Name                             Status    Ports
---- -------------------------------- --------- -------------------------------
1    default                          active    Gi0/4, Gi0/5, Gi0/6, Gi0/7
10   SALES                            active    Gi0/1, Gi0/2
20   ENG                              active    Gi0/3
1002 fddi-default                     act/unsup
1003 token-ring-default               act/unsup
1004 fddinet-default                  act/unsup
1005 trnet-default                    act/unsup
sections.pitfall: Deleting a VLAN that still has ports in it. The ports keep their switchport access vlan setting but become inactive and vanish from show vlan brief, so their hosts silently lose connectivity. Move the ports first, or re-create the VLAN.

activity.title: Build two VLANs
activity.prompt: SW1 needs VLAN 10 named SALES and VLAN 20 named ENG, with G0/1 in VLAN 10 and G0/2 in VLAN 20 as access ports. Configure it, then run show vlan brief and confirm each port left VLAN 1 for the right VLAN.

check.question: You enter switchport access vlan 30 on an access port, but VLAN 30 has not been created. What happens on a typical Catalyst switch?
choices: The command is rejected until you create VLAN 30
The port is assigned but stays err-disabled
The port stays in VLAN 1 until VLAN 30 exists
IOS creates VLAN 30 automatically and assigns the port
check.explanation: IOS prints '% Access VLAN does not exist. Creating vlan 30' and creates it with the default name VLAN0030. It still pays to create and name VLANs explicitly so the names mean something.

sections.title: Naming the VLANs: default, data, voice, native, management
sections.body:
Exam questions and Cisco documents attach labels to VLANs: data VLAN, voice VLAN, native VLAN, management VLAN. These are **roles**, not different kinds of VLAN. Every one of them is an ordinary VLAN number from the same list, used for a particular job.

- **Default VLAN**: VLAN 1, where every port starts. It is a fact about the factory configuration, not a job.
- **Data VLAN** (user VLAN): carries traffic from PCs, printers and servers. Most VLANs you create are data VLANs.
- **Voice VLAN**: carries IP phone traffic, kept apart from data so it can be prioritized. Covered in the next section.
- **Native VLAN**: the one VLAN that an 802.1Q trunk carries untagged. It only means something on trunks. Default: VLAN 1.
- **Management VLAN**: the VLAN in which the switch's own IP address lives, on an SVI such as interface vlan 99, used for SSH, SNMP, syslog and NTP. Default: VLAN 1 (interface vlan 1).
- **Parking VLAN** (sometimes called a black hole VLAN): an unused VLAN with no router and no other ports, where you put unused switch ports so anyone who plugs into a spare jack lands nowhere.

Notice that out of the box the default, native and management VLANs are all VLAN 1. Hardening guides pull them apart: users in their own data VLANs, management on its own VLAN reachable only by administrators, the native VLAN set to an unused number on every trunk, and spare ports parked and shut down. The configuration below shows the management and parking pieces; the native VLAN is set per trunk with switchport trunk native vlan, covered in the Trunking lesson.
sections.code:
! Management VLAN: the switch's own IP address lives here
SW1(config)# vlan 99
SW1(config-vlan)# name MGMT
SW1(config-vlan)# interface vlan 99
SW1(config-if)# ip address 10.1.99.11 255.255.255.0
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# ip default-gateway 10.1.99.1
!
! Parking VLAN: spare ports go nowhere and stay down
SW1(config)# vlan 999
SW1(config-vlan)# name PARKING
SW1(config-vlan)# interface range gigabitethernet0/20 - 23
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 999
SW1(config-if-range)# shutdown
sections.tip: A question that says "native VLAN" is always about trunks. A question that says "management VLAN" is about where the switch's SVI address is.
sections.pitfall: Treating the native VLAN and the default VLAN as the same setting. Both start as VLAN 1, but changing the native VLAN on a trunk moves no access ports, and moving every access port out of VLAN 1 does not change any trunk's native VLAN.

check.question: On a factory-default Cisco switch, which VLAN is the default VLAN, the native VLAN on trunks and the management VLAN?
choices: VLAN 1 for all three
VLAN 1, VLAN 99 and VLAN 1002
VLAN 0 for all three
VLAN 1 for the default VLAN only; the others are unset
check.explanation: VLAN 1 plays all three roles by default: every port starts in it, trunks send it untagged and interface vlan 1 is the default management SVI. That overlap is why best practice moves each role to its own VLAN.

sections.title: Voice VLANs: a phone and a PC on one port
sections.body:
Most offices run one cable to each desk. Cisco IP phones solve the cabling problem with a small **three-port switch built into the phone**: one port faces the wall jack and the access switch, one is the PC port on the back of the phone, and an internal port connects the phone's own CPU. The user's PC plugs into the phone, so two devices now share one switch port. Cisco's design guidance puts them in different VLANs: voice in one, data in another, so voice can be protected and prioritized.

The port is configured as an access port with two VLANs:

- **Data VLAN**: the normal access VLAN, set with `switchport access vlan 10`. The PC's frames travel untagged.
- **Voice VLAN**: set with `switchport voice vlan 11`. The phone tags its own voice frames with an 802.1Q header for VLAN 11, and the 3-bit priority field in that tag carries a class of service (**CoS**) value of 5 by default, so switches can queue voice ahead of data.

How does the phone know to use VLAN 11? The switch tells it through CDP (non-Cisco phones use **LLDP-MED**). CDP is on by default, so it just works; disable CDP on that port and a Cisco phone will not learn its voice VLAN. The same port usually powers the phone with **PoE**, and on Catalyst switches configuring a voice VLAN also enables PortFast on the port automatically.

The port still counts as an access port. The verification has three tells, straight from the official guide:

- show interfaces fa0/4 switchport reports Operational Mode: static access, plus a Voice VLAN line.
- show interfaces trunk does not list the port, because it is not a trunk.
- show interfaces fa0/4 trunk (with the interface named) shows the port as not-trunking but lists both VLANs, 10-11, as allowed and active.

One interaction to remember for later: if you add port security to a phone port, the phone's MAC address is learned in the voice VLAN (and may also be learned in the data VLAN), and the PC adds another. Cisco's guidance is to allow two addresses for the phone plus whatever the data VLAN needs, or the switch will treat the PC as a violation.
sections.code:
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name DATA
SW1(config-vlan)# vlan 11
SW1(config-vlan)# name VOICE
SW1(config-vlan)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 4
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport voice vlan 11
SW1(config-if-range)# end

SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/4 switchport
Name: Fa0/4
Switchport: Enabled
Administrative Mode: static access
Operational Mode: static access
Administrative Trunking Encapsulation: dot1q
Operational Trunking Encapsulation: native
Negotiation of Trunking: Off
Access Mode VLAN: 10 (DATA)
Trunking Native Mode VLAN: 1 (default)
Administrative Native VLAN tagging: enabled
Voice VLAN: 11 (VOICE)
! rest of output omitted

SW1# show interfaces trunk
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/4 trunk

Port        Mode             Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Fa0/4       10-11

sections.pitfall: Configuring the phone port as a trunk so 'both VLANs fit'. The documented design is an access port plus switchport voice vlan; the port stays an access port and the PC stays untagged.

check.question: A port has switchport access vlan 10 and switchport voice vlan 11. How do frames from the phone and from the PC behind it arrive at the switch?
choices: Phone frames tagged with VLAN 11, PC frames untagged in VLAN 10
Both untagged; the switch tells them apart by MAC address
PC frames tagged with VLAN 10, phone frames untagged in VLAN 11
Both tagged, because the port becomes a trunk
check.explanation: The phone learns VLAN 11 from CDP and tags its voice frames with an 802.1Q header for VLAN 11. The PC knows nothing about VLANs and sends untagged frames, which the switch places in the data (access) VLAN 10. The port remains an access port.

sections.title: One VLAN across many switches
sections.body:
VLANs are not limited to one box. Sales people sit on three floors, each floor has its own switch, and you want all of them in VLAN 10. That works as long as two things are true.

First, the switches are joined by a **trunk**: a link that carries many VLANs and tags each frame with its VLAN ID so the next switch knows where it belongs. The Trunking lesson covers trunks in depth. For now, know that an access link between switches carries only one VLAN: if the link between SW1 and SW2 is an access port in VLAN 10, VLAN 20 hosts on the two switches can never reach each other over it. (You could run one access link per VLAN, which the official guide shows as the clumsy alternative: 20 VLANs would burn 20 ports on each switch.)

Second, **every switch the traffic passes through must know the VLAN.** A switch forwards frames only for VLANs that exist and are active in its own VLAN list. This catches people out with transit switches: if SW2 sits between SW1 and SW3 and VLAN 10 was never created on SW2, VLAN 10 frames from SW1 die at SW2, even though SW2 has no VLAN 10 users at all.

Inside each switch, MAC learning and flooding happen per VLAN. When PC1 sends its first frame, SW1 learns PC1's MAC in VLAN 10 on Gi0/1. If the destination is unknown, SW1 floods the frame out every other VLAN 10 port, including the trunk, where it travels with a VLAN 10 tag. SW2 learns PC1's MAC in VLAN 10 on its trunk port and floods to its own VLAN 10 ports. VLAN 20 ports on either switch never see the frame.

The classic Domain 2 picture: SW1 and SW2 each have VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 hosts and one trunk between them. Same-VLAN hosts reach each other across the trunk; different-VLAN hosts do not, even on the same switch.
sections.code:
PC1 (V10)  PC2 (V20)                PC3 (V10)  PC4 (V20)
     |          |                         |          |
   Gi0/1      Gi0/2                     Gi0/1      Gi0/2
  +---------------+  802.1Q trunk    +---------------+
  |      SW1      |Gi0/24 ===== Gi0/24|      SW2      |
  +---------------+  VLANs 10, 20    +---------------+

PC1 <-> PC3  works (same VLAN, crosses the trunk tagged 10)
PC2 <-> PC4  works (same VLAN, crosses the trunk tagged 20)
PC1 <-> PC2  fails without a router (different VLANs)
sections.pitfall: Forgetting to create the VLAN on a switch that only passes the traffic through. No local users does not mean no VLAN: every switch on the path needs it.

activity.title: Same VLAN, different switches
activity.prompt: Put one host in VLAN 10 and one in VLAN 20 on each switch, then test reachability before and after you make the link between the switches a trunk. Notice that the trunk joins matching VLANs across switches but never joins VLAN 10 to VLAN 20.

check.question: VLAN 30 hosts on SW1 and SW3 cannot reach each other. Their traffic passes through SW2 over trunks, SW2 has no VLAN 30 hosts, and show vlan brief on SW2 does not list VLAN 30. What is the fix?
choices: Configure an access port in VLAN 30 on SW2
Change the native VLAN to 30 on both trunks
Nothing; transit switches forward unknown VLANs by default
Create VLAN 30 on SW2
check.explanation: A switch forwards only VLANs that exist and are active locally, even on trunks. Creating VLAN 30 on SW2 lets it carry the traffic between its trunks. No access port is needed, and changing the native VLAN would cause other problems.

sections.title: Verifying where a VLAN reaches
sections.body:
show vlan brief tells you which access ports are in which VLAN on one switch. To prove a VLAN really spans several switches, add three more commands to your habits.

- **show vlan id 10** (or show vlan name SALES) shows a single VLAN. Unlike show vlan brief, its Ports column also lists **trunk ports** that are currently forwarding that VLAN. In the exhibit Gi0/24, the trunk to SW2, appears beside the two access ports.
- **show interfaces status** prints one line per port with its connection state and a Vlan column: a number for an access port, the word **trunk** for a trunk and **routed** for a routed port. It is the fastest way to spot a port that is notconnect, err-disabled or in the wrong VLAN.
- **show mac address-table dynamic vlan 10** lists the MAC addresses learned in VLAN 10 and the port each was learned on. A host on SW2 shows up on SW1's trunk port Gi0/24. If remote hosts never appear on the trunk, VLAN 10 is not crossing it.

Read the exhibit as a story. PC1 and PC2 are local on Gi0/1 and Gi0/2. 0200.2222.0003 is PC3, plugged into SW2, and SW1 learned it through Gi0/24, so VLAN 10 frames are crossing the trunk in both directions. Gi0/3 is in VLAN 20 and Gi0/4 is unused, still in VLAN 1. If PC1 could not reach PC3, you would now check SW2's side, not SW1's.

SW1# show vlan id 10

VLAN Name                             Status    Ports

10   SALES                            active    Gi0/1, Gi0/2, Gi0/24
! VLAN type and MTU table omitted

SW1# show interfaces status

Port      Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi0/1     PC1                connected    10         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/2     PC2                connected    10         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/3     PC5                connected    20         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/4                        notconnect   1            auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/24    Uplink to SW2      connected    trunk      a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX

SW1# show mac address-table dynamic vlan 10
          Mac Address Table
-------------------------------------------

Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----
  10    0200.1111.0001    DYNAMIC     Gi0/1
  10    0200.1111.0002    DYNAMIC     Gi0/2

Total Mac Addresses for this criterion: 3
sections.tip: show vlan brief hides trunks; show vlan id N shows them. If an exhibit uses show vlan id, a trunk port in the list is normal.
sections.pitfall: Concluding that a port missing from show vlan brief is broken. Trunk ports never appear there; check show interfaces status or show interfaces trunk before you assume the port lost its VLAN.

check.question: In show mac address-table vlan 10 on SW1, the MAC address of a VLAN 10 host attached to SW2 appears on SW1 port Gi0/24. What does that tell you?
choices: Gi0/24 is an access port in VLAN 10 on SW1
VLAN 10 frames from that host are arriving at SW1 across the trunk on Gi0/24
The host is misconfigured with a SW1 address
SW1 learned the MAC through CDP
check.explanation: Switches learn source MACs from frames they receive. Seeing a remote host on the trunk port proves that VLAN 10 traffic from SW2 reaches SW1 over that link. CDP plays no part in the MAC address table.

sections.title: VLANs need a router to talk
sections.body:
Two PCs on the same switch, one in VLAN 10 and one in VLAN 20, cannot ping each other. That is not a fault; it is the whole point of a VLAN. They are in different broadcast domains and different subnets, and moving a packet between subnets is routing, a Layer 3 job.

So every VLAN that needs to reach anything else needs a **default gateway**: an IP address on a routing device that sits in that VLAN's subnet. When PC1 (10.1.10.11/24) pings PC3 (10.1.20.13/24), PC1 sees that the destination is in a different subnet and sends the frame to its gateway's MAC address. The router or Layer 3 switch routes the packet into VLAN 20 and delivers it in a new frame with PC3's MAC address. The CCNA tests three ways to provide those gateways, covered fully in the Inter-VLAN Routing lesson:

- **One router interface per VLAN**: each VLAN gets its own access link to its own router port. Simple, but it runs out of ports quickly.
- **Router on a stick (ROAS)**: one router interface on an 802.1Q trunk, with a subinterface per VLAN (`interface g0/0.10`, `encapsulation dot1q 10`, then the gateway address). All inter-VLAN traffic shares that one link.
- **Layer 3 switch with SVIs**: an `interface vlan 10` per VLAN holds the gateway address, and `ip routing` turns routing on. Routing happens in switch hardware, which is why this is the usual campus design.

The same one-VLAN-one-subnet rule shapes DHCP. A DHCP Discover is a broadcast, so it stays inside its VLAN. Each VLAN therefore needs its own address pool, and if the DHCP server sits in another subnet, the gateway interface for that VLAN (the SVI or subinterface) is configured with `ip helper-address` so it relays the request.

When two hosts in different VLANs cannot communicate, think Layer 3 first: does a gateway exist for each VLAN, does each host point to the right gateway, and is routing enabled?
sections.code:
! Option A: Layer 3 switch, one SVI per VLAN as that VLAN's gateway
ip routing
!
interface Vlan10
 ip address 10.1.10.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface Vlan20
 ip address 10.1.20.1 255.255.255.0
!
! Option B: router on a stick, one subinterface per VLAN
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.10
 encapsulation dot1q 10
 ip address 10.1.10.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1q 20
 ip address 10.1.20.1 255.255.255.0
!
! PC1 in VLAN 10: 10.1.10.11/24, gateway 10.1.10.1
! PC3 in VLAN 20: 10.1.20.13/24, gateway 10.1.20.1
sections.tip: An SVI comes up only when its VLAN exists and at least one port in that VLAN is up and forwarding (an access port or a trunk). An SVI stuck down/down usually means the VLAN is missing.
sections.pitfall: Trying to fix a cross-VLAN ping with Layer 2 changes. If the hosts are in different VLANs, look at the gateways and routing, not the trunk.

check.question: PC1 in VLAN 10 and PC2 in VLAN 20 are on the same switch, which has no routing configured. What happens when PC1 pings PC2?
choices: The ping succeeds because both are on the same switch
The ping succeeds only if both ports use switchport mode access
The ping fails; the VLANs need a router or Layer 3 switch acting as gateways
The ping fails until both VLANs are given names
check.explanation: Different VLANs are different subnets, so PC1 sends the packet to its default gateway. With no routing device, nothing can move the packet into VLAN 20. Sharing a physical switch does not matter.

sections.title: Troubleshooting VLAN problems
sections.body:
A user says, 'My PC is connected but I cannot reach anybody.' The link light is on, the port is up/up, and yet nothing works. A very common cause is a port in the wrong VLAN. Work through it in this order:

- Run `show vlan brief` and find the user's port. Is it in the VLAN you expect? Is that VLAN active?
- Run `show interfaces g0/1 switchport` to see one port's administrative and operational mode, access VLAN and voice VLAN.
- Check the VLAN's state. A VLAN can be shut down (`shutdown vlan 10` globally, or `shutdown` in VLAN configuration mode); it then shows act/lshut, and the switch forwards nothing in it.
- If the port is missing from show vlan brief entirely, it is either trunking or assigned to a VLAN that no longer exists. show interfaces switchport tells you which: a deleted VLAN shows as Access Mode VLAN: 30 (Inactive).
- Check the host: an address in that VLAN's subnet and the right default gateway.
- If the VLAN spans switches, confirm it exists on every switch and crosses the trunks (show interfaces trunk, show mac address-table vlan N).

The exhibit is the kind of thing you are looking for: the user on G0/1 should be in SALES (VLAN 10), but the port sits in VLAN 99. One command fixes it.
sections.code:
SW1# show vlan brief

VLAN Name                             Status    Ports
---- -------------------------------- --------- -------------------------------
1    default                          active    Gi0/3, Gi0/4, Gi0/5, Gi0/6
10   SALES                            active    Gi0/2
99   PARKING                          active    Gi0/1
1002 fddi-default                     act/unsup
1003 token-ring-default               act/unsup
1004 fddinet-default                  act/unsup
1005 trnet-default                    act/unsup

SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
sections.pitfall: Looking only at interface status. A port in the wrong VLAN is still up/up, so show ip interface brief looks perfect. VLAN faults hide in show vlan brief and show interfaces switchport.

activity.title: Fix the isolated PC
activity.prompt: The PC on G0/1 should be in VLAN 10 (SALES) but cannot reach its neighbors. Investigate with show vlan brief and show running-config before you change anything, then fix the port without creating any new VLANs.

check.question: A port is up/up, but its host cannot reach anything. show vlan brief lists the port under VLAN 99, while the host's subnet belongs to VLAN 10. Which interface command fixes it?
choices: switchport mode trunk
switchport access vlan 10
no shutdown
name SALES
check.explanation: The port is simply in the wrong VLAN. switchport access vlan 10 moves it into the VLAN that matches the host's subnet. The port is already up, so no shutdown changes nothing, and a trunk is not used for a single PC.

keyTerms.definition: A virtual LAN: a group of switch ports that forms its own broadcast domain, normally mapped to one IP subnet.
The set of devices that receive a broadcast frame sent by any one of them. Each VLAN is one broadcast domain.
A switch port in exactly one data VLAN, connecting an end device that sends untagged frames.
VLAN 1, which every port belongs to out of the box. It cannot be deleted or renamed.
VLAN IDs 1 to 1005, supported by every Catalyst switch and stored in vlan.dat.
VLAN IDs 1006 to 4094, supported on most current switches with some VTP limits.
The access VLAN that carries user traffic; on a phone port it carries the PC's untagged frames.
A second VLAN on an access port for an IP phone, which tags its frames (CoS 5) and learns the VLAN through CDP or LLDP-MED.
The VLAN an 802.1Q trunk carries untagged; VLAN 1 by default and set per trunk.
The VLAN that holds the switch's own IP address on an SVI, used for SSH, SNMP and similar traffic.
An unused VLAN with no gateway where spare ports are placed, usually shut down, so a stray connection reaches nothing.
A link that carries several VLANs, tagging frames with their VLAN ID (802.1Q).
Switch virtual interface (interface vlan N): a logical Layer 3 interface in a VLAN, used for management or as the VLAN's default gateway.
One router interface on an 802.1Q trunk with a subinterface per VLAN, each holding that VLAN's gateway address.
Class of service: the 3-bit priority value in the 802.1Q tag, set to 5 by IP phones for voice.

summary: One VLAN equals one broadcast domain equals one IP subnet.
Normal-range VLANs are 1 to 1005; VLAN 1 is the default and cannot be deleted; move users, management and the native VLAN off it.
vlan 10 and name create a VLAN; switchport mode access and switchport access vlan 10 put a port in it.
switchport voice vlan adds a tagged phone VLAN (CoS 5, learned through CDP) to an access port while the PC stays untagged in the data VLAN.
A VLAN spanning switches needs trunks and must exist on every switch in the path; show vlan id, show interfaces status and the MAC table prove it.
Hosts in different VLANs need a router port per VLAN, router on a stick or a Layer 3 switch with SVIs; check show vlan brief first when a port is up but isolated.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a new help desk hire why two PCs plugged into the same switch might be unable to ping each other, using the words VLAN, broadcast domain, subnet and default gateway, then explain how one cable to a desk can carry both an IP phone and a PC in different VLANs.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a VLAN?
choices: A group of routers that share one routing table
A group of switch ports that forms its own broadcast domain
A wireless network identified by an SSID
A physical cable that carries several subnets
questions.explanation: A VLAN is a logical group of switch ports that acts like a separate LAN, so broadcasts stay inside it. An SSID names a wireless network, and a cable carrying many VLANs is a trunk, not a VLAN.

questions.question: What is the highest normal-range VLAN ID on a Cisco Catalyst switch?
questions.explanation: Normal-range VLANs are 1 to 1005. IDs 1006 to 4094 are the extended range, and 1002 to 1005 are reserved legacy VLANs that cannot be used for ports.

questions.question: Which two statements about the VLANs that exist on a factory-default Catalyst switch are true? (Choose two.)
choices: VLAN 1 cannot be deleted
VLAN 1 is an extended-range VLAN
VLANs 1002 to 1005 cannot be deleted
All ports start in VLAN 1002
VLAN 1 cannot carry user traffic
questions.explanation: VLAN 1 (the default VLAN) and VLANs 1002 to 1005 (legacy FDDI and Token Ring VLANs) are permanent. Ports start in VLAN 1, which can carry user traffic even though best practice moves users elsewhere.

questions.question: You are in interface configuration mode for a PC's switch port. Type the command that assigns the port to VLAN 30.
questions.explanation: switchport access vlan sets the access (data) VLAN of the port. If VLAN 30 does not exist yet, IOS creates it.

questions.question: Type the interface command that makes a port always operate as an access port and stops it negotiating a trunk.
questions.explanation: switchport mode access fixes the administrative mode as access and disables DTP on the port, so it can never become a trunk by negotiation.

questions.question: Starting in privileged EXEC mode, put the commands in order to create VLAN 40 named LAB and place Gi0/5 in it.
questions.explanation: Enter global configuration, create the VLAN, name it inside VLAN configuration mode, move to the interface, assign the access VLAN and leave configuration mode. The name command only works inside VLAN configuration mode, so it must follow vlan 40.

questions.question: Gi0/5 was configured with switchport access vlan 50. Later an engineer entered no vlan 50. Gi0/5 now appears nowhere in show vlan brief. What is the state of Gi0/5?
choices: It moved back to VLAN 1 automatically
It is still assigned to VLAN 50 and is inactive, so it forwards no traffic
It became a trunk because it has no access VLAN
It is err-disabled and must be bounced with shutdown and no shutdown
questions.explanation: Deleting a VLAN does not reassign its ports. They keep the switchport access vlan 50 setting but become inactive until VLAN 50 exists again or the ports are moved, which is why they disappear from show vlan brief.

questions.question: A switch with no routing configured has active access ports in VLANs 1, 10 and 20. How many broadcast domains does it have?
questions.explanation: Each VLAN is a separate broadcast domain, so three VLANs give three broadcast domains. A switch without VLANs would be one broadcast domain no matter how many ports it has.

questions.question: Which three are benefits of dividing a LAN into VLANs? (Choose three.)
choices: Smaller broadcast domains
Eliminating the need for routing between departments
Grouping users by job rather than physical location
Separating voice traffic so it can be prioritized
Increasing the number of MAC addresses a switch can learn
questions.explanation: VLANs shrink broadcast domains, let you group users logically and keep voice apart for QoS. They increase the need for routing (traffic between VLANs must be routed) and do nothing for MAC table size.

questions.question: How does a Cisco IP phone learn which voice VLAN to use on its switch port?
choices: From DHCP option 150
From a VTP advertisement
From CDP messages sent by the switch
It always uses VLAN 1 until reconfigured by hand
questions.explanation: The switch advertises the voice VLAN to the phone in CDP. DHCP option 150 points phones to a TFTP server for their configuration files, not to a VLAN. Without CDP (or LLDP-MED), the phone does not learn the voice VLAN.

questions.question: Port Fa0/7 already has switchport mode access and switchport access vlan 10. Type the interface command that adds VLAN 11 as the voice VLAN.
questions.explanation: switchport voice vlan defines the VLAN the attached IP phone should use. The port stays an access port with data VLAN 10.

questions.question: An engineer says Fa0/4 must be a trunk because it carries two VLANs. Based on the output, which statement is correct?
questions.code:
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/4 switchport
Name: Fa0/4
Switchport: Enabled
Administrative Mode: static access
Operational Mode: static access
Access Mode VLAN: 10 (DATA)
Voice VLAN: 11 (VOICE)
! lines omitted

SW1# show interfaces trunk
SW1#
choices: Fa0/4 is a trunk, but show interfaces trunk hides voice ports
Fa0/4 carries only VLAN 10; the voice VLAN line is ignored on access ports
Fa0/4 is an access port with data VLAN 10 and voice VLAN 11; phone frames are tagged, PC frames are not
Fa0/4 negotiated a trunk with the phone using DTP
questions.explanation: A voice port is an access port (Operational Mode: static access) with an added voice VLAN. The phone tags VLAN 11 frames while the PC's frames are untagged in VLAN 10. That is why show interfaces trunk lists nothing.

questions.question: Two hosts in different VLANs must communicate. What is required?
choices: A trunk between the two hosts' access ports
The same native VLAN on both ports
A voice VLAN on both ports
A Layer 3 device such as a router or Layer 3 switch
questions.explanation: Different VLANs are different subnets, and moving packets between subnets is routing. A router (router on a stick) or a Layer 3 switch with SVIs provides the gateways.

questions.question: PC1 is 10.1.10.11/24 in VLAN 10 with gateway 10.1.10.1. PC3 is 10.1.20.13/24 in VLAN 20. When PC1 pings PC3, which destination MAC address does PC1 put in the frame?
choices: The MAC address of its default gateway
PC3's MAC address, learned with ARP across the VLANs
The broadcast address FFFF.FFFF.FFFF
The switch's own base MAC address
questions.explanation: PC1 sees that 10.1.20.13 is not in its own subnet, so it ARPs for its gateway and sends the frame to the gateway's MAC. ARP broadcasts never cross from VLAN 10 into VLAN 20, so PC1 could not learn PC3's MAC directly.

questions.question: On this Layer 3 switch, VLAN 10 hosts reach their gateway, but interface Vlan20 stays down/down and no VLAN 20 host exists yet. What is the most likely cause?
questions.code:
ip routing
!
vlan 10
 name USERS
!
interface Vlan10
 ip address 10.1.10.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface Vlan20
 ip address 10.1.20.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
choices: ip routing must also be entered under each SVI
VLAN 20 does not exist and has no up ports, so its SVI cannot come up
The Vlan20 subnet overlaps the Vlan10 subnet
An SVI can only be created for VLAN 1
questions.explanation: An SVI needs its VLAN to exist and at least one port in that VLAN up and forwarding. VLAN 20 was never created and no port uses it. ip routing is a global command, and 10.1.10.0/24 and 10.1.20.0/24 do not overlap.

questions.question: Users on Gi0/7 to Gi0/9 lost all connectivity, although the ports are up. Based on the output, what is wrong?
questions.code:
SW1# show vlan brief

VLAN Name                             Status    Ports
---- -------------------------------- --------- -------------------------------
1    default                          active    Gi0/1, Gi0/2, Gi0/3, Gi0/4
10   SALES                            active    Gi0/5, Gi0/6
30   LAB                              act/lshut Gi0/7, Gi0/8, Gi0/9
1002 fddi-default                     act/unsup
! remaining reserved VLANs omitted
choices: VLAN 30 is an unsupported VLAN on this switch
Gi0/7 to Gi0/9 are trunks
VLAN 30 is the native VLAN, so its frames are untagged
VLAN 30 has been shut down, so the switch forwards nothing in it
questions.explanation: act/lshut means the VLAN exists but was shut down locally (shutdown vlan 30 or shutdown in VLAN mode). Re-enable it with no shutdown vlan 30. act/unsup is the different status shown for reserved VLANs 1002 to 1005.

questions.question: Type the show command that lists every VLAN on a switch with its name, status and access ports.
questions.explanation: show vlan brief prints one line per VLAN with its access ports. Trunk ports are not listed because they belong to many VLANs.

questions.question: Type the command that shows Gi0/1's administrative and operational mode, access VLAN and voice VLAN.
questions.explanation: show interfaces <interface> switchport details one port's Layer 2 settings, including Administrative Mode versus Operational Mode, which is how you spot a port that did not do what you configured.

questions.question: Match each term to its description.

pairs.right: Carries one data VLAN to an end device, untagged
Carries many VLANs between switches, tagged
Tagged VLAN an IP phone learns through CDP

questions.explanation: Access ports serve end devices in one VLAN; trunks carry many tagged VLANs; VLAN 1 is the default; the voice VLAN is advertised to phones by CDP; normal-range IDs are 1 to 1005.

questions.question: Why is 'one VLAN, one subnet' the rule of thumb?
questions.answer: Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain, and hosts reach local neighbors with ARP broadcasts. If one subnet spanned two VLANs, ARP could not cross between them, so each VLAN gets its own subnet and a router connects the subnets.
questions.explanation: Linking the Layer 2 boundary (VLAN) to the Layer 3 boundary (subnet) is what makes inter-VLAN routing and DHCP designs predictable.

questions.question: VLAN 10 PCs on SW1 can reach VLAN 10 PCs on SW2, but VLAN 20 PCs on the two switches cannot reach each other. Both switches show this for G0/24, the only link between them. What is the most likely problem?
questions.code:
SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/24 switchport
Name: Gi0/24
Switchport: Enabled
Administrative Mode: static access
Operational Mode: static access
Access Mode VLAN: 10 (SALES)
! lines omitted
choices: VLAN 20 is shut down on both switches
The link between the switches is an access port in VLAN 10, so only VLAN 10 crosses it
G0/24 needs a voice VLAN to carry a second VLAN
VLAN 20 PCs need VLAN 1 as their default gateway
questions.explanation: An access link carries exactly one VLAN, here VLAN 10. To carry VLANs 10 and 20 between switches, G0/24 must be an 802.1Q trunk on both ends.

questions.question: A PC cannot reach other hosts in its own VLAN on the same switch. Which two commands best confirm whether its port is in the correct VLAN? (Choose two.)
choices: show ip route
show vlan brief
show ip interface brief
show interfaces gi0/1 switchport
show cdp neighbors
questions.explanation: show vlan brief lists ports per VLAN, and show interfaces switchport shows one port's access VLAN and mode. show ip interface brief only shows up/down status, which looks fine for a port in the wrong VLAN, and show cdp neighbors and show ip route say nothing about VLAN membership.

questions.question: Why do best practices recommend moving user ports out of VLAN 1?
choices: VLAN 1 cannot carry IP traffic
VLAN 1 frames are always dropped on trunks
VLAN 1 is the default everywhere, so unconfigured ports and control traffic share it, which widens the attack surface
VLAN 1 is limited to 24 ports per switch
questions.explanation: Every port starts in VLAN 1 and control protocols use it by default, so users left there share a VLAN with any unconfigured port an intruder plugs into. VLAN 1 itself works normally; the issue is exposure, not function.

questions.question: On a lab switch you ran erase startup-config and reload, but show vlan brief still lists VLANs 10 and 20. Why?
choices: Normal-range VLANs are stored in flash:vlan.dat, which erase startup-config does not remove
VLANs 10 and 20 were relearned from the native VLAN after the reload
The reload did not finish, so the VLANs are still in RAM
VLANs are kept in NVRAM and can never be removed
questions.explanation: The VLAN database lives in vlan.dat in flash. To return a lab switch to defaults you erase the startup config and also delete flash:vlan.dat before reloading.

questions.question: A port has switchport access vlan 10 and switchport voice vlan 110. In which VLAN does the PC plugged into the phone's PC port send its traffic? (Number only.)
questions.explanation: The PC sends untagged frames, which the switch places in the access (data) VLAN, 10. Only the phone uses voice VLAN 110.

questions.question: A port has switchport access vlan 10 but no switchport mode command, and the switch defaults to dynamic auto. Someone plugs in a switch whose port is set to dynamic desirable. What can happen?
choices: Nothing; switchport access vlan disables DTP
The port negotiates a trunk with DTP, exposing every VLAN to the new switch
The port becomes err-disabled
Both switches put the link in VLAN 10 and ignore DTP
questions.explanation: Without switchport mode access the port stays dynamic auto, and dynamic auto plus dynamic desirable forms a trunk. Hard-coding switchport mode access disables DTP and prevents this.

questions.question: What kind of link lets both VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 extend from SW1 to SW2 over a single cable?
choices: An access link in VLAN 1
A voice VLAN link
A routed port
An 802.1Q trunk
questions.explanation: A trunk tags each frame with its VLAN ID, so one link carries many VLANs. An access link carries only one, and a routed port does not carry VLANs at all.

questions.question: Match each show vlan brief observation to its meaning.

pairs.right: VLAN exists but is shut down on this switch
Port is trunking or its VLAN no longer exists

questions.explanation: Reading status values quickly is half of VLAN troubleshooting: lshut means locally shut down, unsup marks the reserved legacy VLANs, and a missing port is either a trunk or an orphan of a deleted VLAN.

questions.question: An engineer says Gi0/24 must have been added to VLAN 10 as an access port by mistake. Based on the output, which statement is correct?
questions.code:
SW1# show vlan id 10

VLAN Name                             Status    Ports
---- -------------------------------- --------- -------------------------------
10   SALES                            active    Gi0/1, Gi0/2, Gi0/24

SW1# show interfaces status | include Gi0/24
Gi0/24    Uplink to SW2      connected    trunk      a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
choices: Gi0/24 is an access port in VLAN 10 and should be moved
Gi0/24 is a trunk forwarding VLAN 10; show vlan id lists trunks as well as access ports
Gi0/24 is err-disabled, so it is listed under the last VLAN it used
VLAN 10 is the native VLAN, which is why the trunk appears
questions.explanation: show vlan id (unlike show vlan brief) lists trunk ports that are forwarding the VLAN. show interfaces status confirms Gi0/24 is a trunk, so seeing it beside the VLAN 10 access ports is normal and shows VLAN 10 is carried toward SW2.

questions.question: In show interfaces status, what does the word trunk in the Vlan column of a port mean?
choices: The port is operating as a trunk carrying multiple VLANs
The port is in VLAN 1, the default VLAN
The port is a routed port with an IP address
The port carries only the native VLAN
questions.explanation: The Vlan column shows the access VLAN number for access ports, trunk for ports operating as trunks and routed for routed ports. The native VLAN is shown by show interfaces trunk, not here.

questions.question: Match each VLAN role to its description.

pairs.right: Holds the switch's own SVI address
Tagged VLAN used by IP phones
Unused VLAN for shut-down spare ports

questions.explanation: These are jobs given to ordinary VLAN numbers. On a factory-default switch the default, native and management roles all fall on VLAN 1, which is why hardening guides separate them.

questions.question: Which three steps follow best practice for unused switch ports? (Choose three.)
choices: Configure switchport mode access
Leave the port in VLAN 1 so it works if someone needs it
Assign the port to an unused parking VLAN
Shut the port down
Set the port to dynamic desirable
questions.explanation: Hard-coding access mode stops DTP, a parking VLAN means nothing useful is reachable, and shutdown keeps the port dark until it is needed. Leaving ports in VLAN 1 or dynamic mode is exactly what an intruder hopes for.

questions.question: Based on this output from SW1, out which port does SW1 forward a unicast frame in VLAN 10 sent to MAC 0200.2222.0003?
questions.code:
SW1# show mac address-table dynamic vlan 10
          Mac Address Table
-------------------------------------------

Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----
  10    0200.1111.0001    DYNAMIC     Gi0/1
  10    0200.1111.0002    DYNAMIC     Gi0/2
  10    0200.2222.0003    DYNAMIC     Gi0/24
Total Mac Addresses for this criterion: 3
choices: It floods the frame out every VLAN 10 port
Gi0/1
Gi0/24, the trunk toward SW2
It drops the frame because the host is on another switch
questions.explanation: The MAC table maps 0200.2222.0003 in VLAN 10 to Gi0/24, so the frame leaves through the trunk to SW2, where that host lives. The switch floods only when the destination is unknown.

questions.question: Fa0/4 connects an IP phone with a PC behind it. Which statement explains this output?
questions.code:
SW1# show interfaces trunk
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/4 trunk

Port        Mode             Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Fa0/4       off              802.1q         not-trunking  1

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Fa0/4       10-11

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Fa0/4       10-11
choices: Fa0/4 is a broken trunk and needs switchport mode trunk
Fa0/4 negotiated a trunk with the phone using DTP
Fa0/4 carries only VLAN 1 because it is not trunking
Fa0/4 is an access port with data VLAN 10 and voice VLAN 11, which is why both VLANs are listed
questions.explanation: A voice port is an access port, so show interfaces trunk lists nothing. Naming the interface in show interfaces fa0/4 trunk reveals that it is not trunking yet allows both the data VLAN (10) and the voice VLAN (11), because the phone tags VLAN 11 frames.

questions.question: By default, which Layer 2 CoS value does a Cisco IP phone put in the 802.1Q tag of its voice frames? (Number only.)
questions.explanation: Cisco IP phones mark voice with CoS 5 in the 3-bit priority field of the 802.1Q tag (and IP precedence 5 in the IP header), so switches can queue voice ahead of data.

questions.question: After this change, the IP phones on these ports get addresses from the data subnet and the PCs behind them get addresses from the voice subnet. VLAN 10 is DATA and VLAN 11 is VOICE. What is wrong?
questions.code:
interface range FastEthernet0/1 - 24
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 11
 switchport voice vlan 10
choices: The ports must be trunks to carry two VLANs
The access and voice VLAN numbers are swapped
switchport voice vlan requires VLAN 1 as the data VLAN
CDP must be disabled for the phones to use the voice VLAN
questions.explanation: switchport access vlan sets the data VLAN used by the untagged PC, and switchport voice vlan sets the VLAN the phone tags. Here the numbers are swapped, so the phone is told to use VLAN 10 and the PC lands in VLAN 11. Swap them back.

questions.question: Type the command that shows only VLAN 10, including the trunk ports currently forwarding it.
questions.explanation: show vlan id 10 prints one VLAN. Its Ports column includes trunks that carry the VLAN, which show vlan brief leaves out.

questions.question: Which three designs let hosts in VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 communicate? (Choose three.)
choices: A router with one physical interface in each VLAN
A trunk between the two access switches
A router with 802.1Q subinterfaces on a trunk (router on a stick)
A Layer 3 switch with an SVI per VLAN and ip routing enabled
Setting both VLANs as native VLANs on the uplink
questions.explanation: Any Layer 3 device with an interface in each VLAN works: separate router ports, router-on-a-stick subinterfaces on a trunk, or SVIs on a Layer 3 switch with ip routing. A trunk or a shared native VLAN only extends VLANs; it never joins two of them.

questions.question: PC2 (VLAN 20, SW1 Gi0/2) cannot reach PC4 (meant to be in VLAN 20, SW2 Gi0/2). VLAN 10 hosts work across the trunk, which allows all VLANs. Based on SW2's output, what is the problem?
questions.code:
SW2# show vlan brief

VLAN Name                             Status    Ports
---- -------------------------------- --------- -------------------------------
1    default                          active    Gi0/2, Gi0/3, Gi0/4
10   SALES                            active    Gi0/1
1002 fddi-default                     act/unsup
1003 token-ring-default               act/unsup
1004 fddinet-default                  act/unsup
1005 trnet-default                    act/unsup
choices: The trunk must be reconfigured to allow VLAN 20
VLAN 20 is shut down on SW2
VLAN 20 does not exist on SW2 and Gi0/2 is still in VLAN 1
Gi0/2 is a trunk port, so it is hidden from VLAN 20
questions.explanation: VLAN 20 does not exist on SW2, and Gi0/2 is still in VLAN 1, so PC4 sits in a different broadcast domain from PC2. Create VLAN 20 on SW2 and put Gi0/2 in it. The trunk is fine, since VLAN 10 crosses it.

questions.question: PC1 (VLAN 10) pings PC3 (VLAN 20) through a Layer 3 switch with SVIs for both VLANs. Put the events in order, starting after PC1 already knows its gateway's MAC address.
items: PC1 sees that PC3 is in a different subnet
PC1 sends the frame to the MAC address of the Vlan10 SVI
The Layer 3 switch looks up 10.1.20.13 and finds the connected route on Vlan20
The switch ARPs for PC3 in VLAN 20 if it does not already know the MAC
The switch forwards a new frame in VLAN 20 to PC3
questions.explanation: The host sends to its gateway because the destination is off-subnet, the Layer 3 switch routes between its SVIs, uses ARP in VLAN 20 if needed, and builds a new frame for the destination VLAN.
